title: Where it didn't

segments.voice: Yesterday: where it worked, as the Discourses promised it would. Your line was it worked here. Did you write down the moment you found, with the day or the place? Keep it close. Today we turn it over. Day six hundred ninety-four.

Nobody makes a poster of this part. Three in the morning, a year into the practice, someone lies awake who knows all the lines by now. Some things are up to us, some aren't. It isn't the thing, it's the judgment about the thing. They could recite them in their sleep, if they could sleep. And none of it is loosening the knot in the chest. The words sit there like a poster on a waiting-room wall. Yesterday we named where the porch helped. Today, just as plainly: where it didn't.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `ALL THE LINES, NO SLEEP.` → `WHERE IT DIDN'T HELP.`

segments.voice: First, the Stoics saw this coming. In the Discourses, Epictetus challenges his students: show me a Stoic, if you can. Not someone who can talk Stoic, but someone who is sick and happy, in danger and happy, disgraced and happy. He says he'd gladly see one, and implies he hasn't. And Marcus, writing to himself, expects to be knocked out of tune. When circumstances force you to be disturbed, he says, come back to yourself quickly, and don't stay out of tune longer than you must. We met that line on day five hundred seventy-five. The teachers didn't claim the method always worked, even on them. Second, where it can misfire. When it turns into small-s stoic: teeth gritted, feelings pushed down until they come out sideways. When up to us and not up to us becomes an excuse to shrug at something you could change, or something unfair that someone should challenge. And when the trouble is depression, a deep loss, or a body that needs care. A maxim is not a doctor, a friend, or a night's sleep. Third, two honest reasons. Sometimes the tool was fine and you were hungry, exhausted, or alone. Sometimes the tool was the wrong one for the job. Both are worth knowing, and neither is a failure of character. Fourth, why say it out loud. A practice that only reports its wins turns into a sales pitch. One that can say here, it didn't help stays a practice, something you use with open eyes.
screen: `SHOW ME A STOIC, IF YOU CAN.` · `WHERE IT CAN MISFIRE.` · `TIRED, OR THE WRONG TOOL.` · `HONESTY KEEPS IT A PRACTICE.` · then, large: `HONEST ABOUT IT.`

segments.voice: Let one moment come where the porch didn't help. Choose one you can look at today; you don't have to open the heaviest one. Where were you? What did you reach for, and what happened? Then ask, gently: was I tired, hungry, alone? Or was this the wrong tool? Don't judge the answer. Just name it. If what comes up is heavy and still with you, that's a reason to talk to someone you trust, not to try harder alone. The bell holds the time.
Small-s stoic, when the practice curdles into teeth gritted and feelings pushed down until they come out sideways. Today's word.

Your line: honest about it. Next to yesterday's moment, write today's, in one sentence. Then add one thing that might help next time, whether it's sleep, a person, or a different tool. Day six hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism look honestly at where it hasn't helped, and pair it with other support, such as friends, counseling, rest or a faith community.

fork.setup: you're one of Epictetus's students. he asks the room to show him one person who is sick and happy, in danger and happy, disgraced and happy. what happens?
options: he implies nobody there can show him one
fork.reveal: Discourses 2.19: he says he'd gladly see such a Stoic, and the way he asks makes clear he hasn't yet. the teacher names the gap himself.

trapdoor: what you thought: if the practice is real, it should always work.
what it means: the porch has limits, and naming them, without blame, keeps it honest.
what a scholar hears: Epictetus asks to be shown a single Stoic (Discourses 2.19), and Marcus expects to be put out of tune and asks only to return quickly (Meditations 6.11).

notes: Discourses 2.19 paraphrased: 'show me a Stoic', sick and happy, in danger and happy, dying and happy, disgraced and happy. Confirm section numbers and the list.
Practice and carry point toward support (people, rest) for heavy moments; the script avoids presenting Stoicism as a substitute for medical or mental-health care.
